title: `PartitionViewOp` needs to define shape twice, this is redundant
body:
For example in [sync.py](https://github.com/zhangstevenunity/PTOAS/blob/2c8d83ea0ea1ca748ce53d178bef6878e644d113/test/samples/Sync/sync.py) and most of other examples:

The shape is first declared in `pto.PartitionTensorViewType.get(shape=[32, 32], element_type=f32)`

https://github.com/zhangstevenunity/PTOAS/blob/2c8d83ea0ea1ca748ce53d178bef6878e644d113/test/samples/Sync/sync.py#L17

But again in

https://github.com/zhangstevenunity/PTOAS/blob/2c8d83ea0ea1ca748ce53d178bef6878e644d113/test/samples/Sync/sync.py#L46-L47

The generated IR also have both `[%c32, %c32]` and `<32x32xf32>`. This is redundant information.

```
    %2 = pto.partition_view %0, offsets = [%c0, %c0], sizes = [%c32, %c32] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?xf32> -> !pto.partition_tensor_view<32x32xf32>
    %3 = pto.partition_view %1, offsets = [%c0, %c0], sizes = [%c32, %c32] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?xf32> -> !pto.partition_tensor_view<32x32xf32>
```

Better be like `tv2_f32 = pto.TensorViewType.get(shape_or_rank=2, element_type=f32)` that only specifies rank
https://github.com/zhangstevenunity/PTOAS/blob/2c8d83ea0ea1ca748ce53d178bef6878e644d113/test/samples/Sync/sync.py#L16

Then the IR is less redundant
```
    %0 = pto.make_tensor_view %arg0, shape = [%c32, %c32] strides = [%c32, %c1] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?xf32>
    %1 = pto.make_tensor_view %arg1, shape = [%c32, %c32] strides = [%c32, %c1] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?xf32>
```

title: Support Scalar memref.load End-to-End (Python Binding → EmitC Lowering)
body:
Currently, the pipeline lacks clear end-to-end support for scalar memory accesses expressed via memref.load, especially when building IR from Python and lowering to EmitC / C codegen.

In MLIR, scalar loads are naturally modeled using memref.load, where the result type is a scalar (e.g., f16, f32, i32). This is the canonical way to express element-wise memory access and is widely used across MLIR dialects. The Python binding already exposes this via memref.LoadOp(memref, indices).result, enabling Python-based kernel construction to express scalar reads cleanly.

However, downstream lowering paths (e.g., bufferization → EmitC) do not consistently handle scalar memref.load. In particular, EmitC lowering should translate scalar loads into appropriate pointer dereference semantics (or equivalent helper calls), preserving address spaces and element types.

This issue proposes:
Adding EmitC lowering rules that map scalar loads to valid C/EmitC constructs.

Including tests covering Python → MLIR → EmitC for scalar load/store patterns.

This would enable clean expression of scalar access patterns, boundary handling, and mixed scalar/tile kernels without introducing custom scalar load ops.

body:
#63 Adds splitk FA test which triggers some bugs in `insert-sync` pass.

## 1. 目录结构

| `flash_attention_full_intermediate.pto` | 完整中间版本 |

### npu_validation/ — 测试基础设施:
| 文件 | 说明 |
|------|------|
| `run.sh` | 端到端测试脚本 (golden.py → cmake build → run → compare.py) |
| `golden.py` | 生成随机 32×32 float32 矩阵 (seed=19)，计算 golden reference |
| `compare.py` | 比较 golden_v6.bin vs v6.bin，容差 1e-3 |
| `CMakeLists.txt` | Bisheng 编译器构建配置，目标 Ascend910B1 |
| `main.cpp` | ACL 测试驱动: init → alloc → load data → launch 3 kernels → copy back → write output |
| `launch.cpp` | 通用 kernel launch wrapper |
| `launch_qk.cpp` | QK kernel launch wrapper |
| `launch_softmax.cpp` | Softmax kernel launch wrapper |
| `launch_sv.cpp` | SV kernel launch wrapper |

## 2. 编译与测试方法

### 编译命令

```bash
PTOAS=/data/sunwenbo/pto/llvm-workspace/PTOAS/build/tools/ptoas/ptoas

# 编译 3 个 kernel (必须使用 --enable-insert-sync)
$PTOAS --enable-insert-sync flash_attention_qk.pto -o flash_attention_qk.cpp
$PTOAS --enable-insert-sync flash_attention_softmax.pto -o flash_attention_softmax.cpp
$PTOAS --enable-insert-sync flash_attention_sv.pto -o flash_attention_sv.cpp

# 复制到 npu_validation 目录
cp flash_attention_qk.cpp npu_validation/flash_attention_qk_kernel.cpp
cp flash_attention_softmax.cpp npu_validation/flash_attention_softmax_kernel.cpp
cp flash_attention_sv.cpp npu_validation/flash_attention_sv_kernel.cpp
```

### 运行测试

```bash
cd npu_validation && bash run.sh
```

测试流程:
1. `golden.py` 生成随机输入矩阵和 golden reference
2. CMake + Bisheng 编译 kernel 和测试驱动
3. 在 Ascend NPU 上运行
4. `compare.py` 比较输出与 golden reference

## 3. 测试结果

| 编译方式 | max diff | 结果 |
|----------|----------|------|
| 不使用 `--enable-insert-sync` | 72.82 | FAIL (无同步指令) |
| 使用 `--enable-insert-sync` | 78.80 | FAIL (同步位置错误) |

- Golden 值范围: [0.99, 2.93]，NPU 输出范围: [-29.03, 79.58]
- 937/1024 个元素差异 > 1.0

## 3. Bug 分析

### 根因: Softmax Kernel 中的两个同步 Bug

QK 和 SV kernel (matmul 流水线) 的同步正确，问题仅出在 softmax kernel (vector 流水线)。

**Bug 1: `wait_flag` 位置过晚**

```cpp
TLOAD(v40, v29);                                    // Line 60: PIPE_MTE2
set_flag(PIPE_MTE2, PIPE_V, EVENT_ID0);             // Line 61
// ← wait_flag 应该在这里 (Bug 1: vector 操作前缺少 wait)
TMULS(v40, v40, v12);                               // Line 62: PIPE_V - 在 wait 之前使用了 v40!
TMAXS(v40, v40, v11);                               // Line 63
TMINS(v40, v40, v10);                               // Line 64
TMUL(v42, v40, v40);                                // Line 65
TMUL(v43, v42, v40);                                // Line 66
TMUL(v44, v43, v40);                                // Line 67
TMULS(v42, v42, v7);                                // Line 68
TMULS(v43, v43, v6);                                // Line 69
TMULS(v44, v44, v5);                                // Line 70
wait_flag(PIPE_MTE2, PIPE_V, EVENT_ID0);            // Line 71: ← 太晚了!
```

**Bug 2: `set_flag` 位置过早**

```cpp
TADD(v41, v41, v44);                                // Line 74
set_flag(PIPE_V, PIPE_MTE3, EVENT_ID0);             // Line 75: ← 太早了! (Bug 2)
TADDS(v41, v41, v9);                                // Line 76: 还在计算!
TDIVS(v41, v41, v8);                                // Line 77: 还在计算!
wait_flag(PIPE_V, PIPE_MTE3, EVENT_ID0);            // Line 78
TSTORE(v39, v41);                                   // Line 79
```

- **Bug 1**: 将 `wait_flag(PIPE_MTE2, PIPE_V, EVENT_ID0)` 从 line 71 移到 line 61-62 之间
- **Bug 2**: 将 `set_flag(PIPE_V, PIPE_MTE3, EVENT_ID0)` 从 line 75 移到 line 77 之后

title: New features need to support
body:
1. On A5, hardware provides a new sync mechanism called "buffer id", the cce code looks like:
uint8_t bufId = 0;
get_buf(PIPE_MTE2, bufId, 0); // The subsequent MTE2 instructions can only be executed after get_buf acquires the lock.
DataCopyToL1();  // MTE2
rls_buf(PIPE_MTE2, bufId, 0); // Release the lock so that other get_buf can acquire the lock.

get_buf(PIPE_MTE1, bufId, 0); // The subsequent MTE1 instructions can only be executed after get_buf acquires the lock.
DataCopyToL0();  // MTE1
rls_buf(PIPE_MTE1, bufId, 0); // Release the lock

This mechanism does not require users to provide two pipelines that wait for each other. Users only need to acquire a buf id when they want to use a particular pipeline, which greatly improves usability. Additionally, the number of buf ids is 27, which exceeds the 8 event ids.

So we want ptoas to provide interfaces that allow programmar to manually insert sync by buffer id.

2. The first version block-based programing will be pulished on A5, so it's best to verify the functionality and accuracy of the ptoas interface on A5 hardware before 2.28

3. For ease of debugging, we need to provide printf and trap interfaces. The printf interface supports printing arbitrary constant strings, integers, and floating-point numbers. Trap is a native hardware capability（in cce trap()） that can report aicerror and can be used for branch checking and binary search.

title: Tile Op reoder to do VF fusion
body:
Tile Fusion 主要针对以下两类 PTO 指令序列进行优化：
● 存在依赖关系（Producer-Consumer）：对于前后有依赖的 PTO指令，经过 Tile Fusion 后会将多个PTO指令融合成一个 VF，并优化掉对 UB (Unified Buffer) 的 Load/Store 指令。
● 无依赖关系（Independent Ops）：对于没有依赖的 PTO指令，Tile Fusion 也会将多个PTO指令融合成一个 VF，降低 VF Launch 开销。

title: ptoas segfault on the latest commit due to EmitC changes
[PTO][Lowering] subset lowering forces contiguous child strides and may break address semantics
body:
### Problem
`pto.subset` is described as a strided view inheriting source strides, but lowering rewrites result strides to contiguous `[child_width, 1]`.

### Evidence
- ODS description says inherited strides: `include/PTO/IR/PTOOps.td:168`
- Lowering hardcodes child strides:
  - `lib/PTO/Transforms/PTOViewToMemref.cpp:527`
  - `lib/PTO/Transforms/PTOViewToMemref.cpp:533`
  - `lib/PTO/Transforms/PTOViewToMemref.cpp:542`

### Repro
```bash
build/tools/ptoas/ptoas test/samples/_out/Subset/subset-pto-ir.pto
```

Observed lowering output includes:
- parent: `memref<32x64xf32, strided<[64, 1], ...>`
- child subset: `to memref<32x32xf32, strided<[32, 1], ...>`

### Why this is risky
For parent `32x64` and child `32x32`, row step changes from 64 to 32, so address formula changes for rows > 0.

### Expected behavior
Either:
1. Preserve view semantics by keeping source-compatible strides, or
2. Explicitly materialize contiguous memory (alloc+copy) if contiguous child layout is intended.

### Acceptance criteria
- Decide and document canonical subset semantics.
- Align ODS docs + lowering implementation.
- Add regression test proving row-stride correctness for `32x64 -> subset 32x32`.

title: [PTO][IR] CopyOp::getPipe uses srcSpace in isDstGlobal condition
body:
### Problem
`CopyOp::getPipe()` appears to contain a typo in destination-global detection.

### Evidence
`lib/PTO/IR/PTO.cpp:6310`
```cpp
bool isDstGlobal = (dstSpace == AddressSpace::GM || srcSpace == AddressSpace::MAT);
```
The second disjunct likely should be `dstSpace == AddressSpace::MAT`.

### Impact
PIPE routing may be incorrect for some copy routes (especially when destination is MAT but source is not MAT).

### Expected behavior
Use destination space consistently:
```cpp
bool isDstGlobal = (dstSpace == AddressSpace::GM || dstSpace == AddressSpace::MAT);
```

### Acceptance criteria
- Fix condition.
- Add route test(s) for combinations involving `dst=MAT` and `dst=GM`.
- Verify resulting `getPipe()` matches intended MTE2/MTE3 behavior.

### Expected behavior
Decide one canonical syntax and keep docs/parser/tests aligned.
- Option A: parser accepts docs positional syntax
- Option B: docs switch to keyworded syntax (current parser behavior)

### Acceptance criteria
- Canonical syntax documented.
- Parser behavior aligned to canonical syntax.
- lit parser tests for accepted + rejected variants.

title: 2D dynamic view of tensor leads to valid cpp code for bisheng & CANN 8.5.0 ISA header
body:
When attempting to create a 2D dynamic-shape tensor (`argN` below is passed at run-time):

```python
        arg0, arg1, arg2, argN = entry.arguments
        total_elements = arith.IndexCastOp(IndexType.get(), argN).result
        tv0 = pto.MakeTensorViewOp(tensor_type, arg0, [c1, total_elements], [total_elements, c1]).result
```

`ptoas` runs fine, but the generated cpp gets error when compiled by `bisheng`:

```
In file included from /usr/local/Ascend/cann-8.5.0/include/pto/pto-inst.hpp:19:
/usr/local/Ascend/cann-8.5.0/include/pto/common/pto_tile.hpp:137:9: error: static assertion failed due to requirement '(-1 == DYNAMIC) + (-1 == DYNAMIC) + (-1 == DYNAMIC) + (-1 == DYNAMIC) + (1 == DYNAMIC) == GlobalTensorDim::DIM_1': 1-parameter constructors is only applicable to Stride with 1 dynamic dimension.
        static_assert((SN1 == DYNAMIC) + (SN2 == DYNAMIC) + (SN3 == DYNAMIC) + (SN4 == DYNAMIC) + (SN5 == DYNAMIC) ==
        ^             ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
./add.cpp:184:11: note: in instantiation of member function 'pto::Stride<-1, -1, -1, -1, 1>::Stride' requested here
    v70 = pto::Stride<-1, -1, -1, -1, 1>(v31);
```

```bash
    -Wno-macro-redefined -Wno-ignored-attributes -fstack-protector-strong \
    -xcce -Xhost-start -Xhost-end \
    -mllvm -cce-aicore-stack-size=0x8000 \
```

Full `add_builder.py` script:

```python
from mlir.ir import Context, Location, Module, InsertionPoint, IntegerType
from mlir.ir import F32Type, IndexType
from mlir.dialects import func, arith, scf, pto


def build():
    with Context() as ctx, Location.unknown():
        pto.register_dialect(ctx, load=True)

        m = Module.create()

        f32 = F32Type.get()
        i32 = IntegerType.get_signless(32)
        u32 = IntegerType.get_signless(32)
        ptr_f32 = pto.PtrType.get(f32)

        tensor_type = pto.TensorViewType.get(2, f32)

        tile_length = 1024
        view_type = pto.PartitionTensorViewType.get([1, tile_length], f32)
        vec = pto.AddressSpaceAttr.get(pto.AddressSpace.VEC)
        bl = pto.BLayoutAttr.get(pto.BLayout.RowMajor)
        sl = pto.SLayoutAttr.get(pto.SLayout.NoneBox)
        pd = pto.PadValueAttr.get(pto.PadValue.Null)

        cfg = pto.TileBufConfigAttr.get(bl, sl, 512, pd)

        tile_type = pto.TileBufType.get([1, tile_length], f32, vec, [1, tile_length], cfg)
        fn_ty = func.FunctionType.get([ptr_f32, ptr_f32, ptr_f32, u32], [])

        with InsertionPoint(m.body):
            fn = func.FuncOp("vec_add_1d_dynamic", fn_ty)
            entry = fn.add_entry_block()

        with InsertionPoint(entry):
            c0 = arith.ConstantOp(IndexType.get(), 0).result
            c1 = arith.ConstantOp(IndexType.get(), 1).result
            c1024 = arith.ConstantOp(IndexType.get(), tile_length).result

            arg0, arg1, arg2, argN = entry.arguments

            cid = pto.GetBlockIdxOp().result
            sub_bid = pto.GetSubBlockIdxOp().result
            sub_bnum = pto.GetSubBlockNumOp().result
            cidmul = arith.MulIOp(cid, sub_bnum).result
            vid = arith.AddIOp(cidmul, sub_bid).result
            num_blocks = pto.GetBlockNumOp().result

            # NOTE: convert i64, i32 all to index type for avoid type mismatch for arith ops
            vid_idx = arith.IndexCastOp(IndexType.get(), vid).result
            num_blocks_idx = arith.IndexCastOp(IndexType.get(), num_blocks).result
            total_elements = arith.IndexCastOp(IndexType.get(), argN).result

            elements_per_core = arith.DivUIOp(total_elements, num_blocks_idx).result
            num_tiles = arith.DivUIOp(elements_per_core, c1024).result

            vec_section = pto.SectionVectorOp()
            vec_block = vec_section.body.blocks.append()
            with InsertionPoint(vec_block):

                tv0 = pto.MakeTensorViewOp(tensor_type, arg0, [c1, total_elements], [total_elements, c1]).result
                tv1 = pto.MakeTensorViewOp(tensor_type, arg1, [c1, total_elements], [total_elements, c1]).result
                tv2 = pto.MakeTensorViewOp(tensor_type, arg2, [c1, total_elements], [total_elements, c1]).result

                tb0 = pto.AllocTileOp(tile_type).result
                tb1 = pto.AllocTileOp(tile_type).result
                tb2 = pto.AllocTileOp(tile_type).result

                # for loop: for i in range(num_tiles)
                # TODO: use `scf.for_` syntax sugar https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/llvmorg-19.1.7/mlir/python/mlir/dialects/scf.py#L106
                loop = scf.ForOp(c0, num_tiles, c1)
                with InsertionPoint(loop.body):
                    i = loop.induction_variable
                    offset_core = arith.MulIOp(vid_idx, elements_per_core).result
                    offset_tile = arith.MulIOp(i, c1024).result
                    offset_global = arith.AddIOp(offset_core, offset_tile).result

                    sv0 = pto.PartitionViewOp(
                        view_type, tv0, offsets=[c0, offset_global], sizes=[c1, c1024]
                    ).result
                    sv1 = pto.PartitionViewOp(
                        view_type, tv1, offsets=[c0, offset_global], sizes=[c1, c1024]
                    ).result
                    sv2 = pto.PartitionViewOp(
                        view_type, tv2, offsets=[c0, offset_global], sizes=[c1, c1024]
                    ).result

                    pto.TLoadOp(None, sv0, tb0)
                    pto.TLoadOp(None, sv1, tb1)
                    pto.TAddOp(tb0, tb1, tb2)
                    pto.TStoreOp(None, tb2, sv2)

                    scf.YieldOp([])

            func.ReturnOp([])

        m.operation.verify()
        return m


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(build())
```

```cpp
extern "C" void call_kernel(
    void *stream, uint8_t *x, uint8_t *y, uint8_t *z, int32_t N)
{
```

title: How to reuse buffer space for `pto.AllocTileOp` with varying valid_row/valid_col ?
body:
In https://github.com/huawei-csl/pto-dsl/pull/12 I made an arbitrary-dynamic-shape kernel example by masking-out out-of-bound tiles and elements.

However, I had to adjust `valid_col` inside the for-loop:

```python
for i in scf.for_(c0, tiles_to_process, c1):
    ...
    # change`c_tile_actual` according to remaining elements
    tb0 = pto.AllocTileOp(
        tile_buf_dynamic, valid_row=c1, valid_col=c_tile_actual
    ).result
```

Because `AllocTileOp` is lowered to new `Tile` allocation + `TASSIGN`, VEC UB space is wasted, not reused across iterations.

Note that buffer-reuse is doable if I don't need to adjust `valid_shape`, ref this less-flexible version of dynamic shape kernel: https://github.com/huawei-csl/pto-dsl/pull/11. **But supporting arbitrary shape is very important for practical use cases, such as for dynamic batch dim and sequence dim.**

## Proposed solution

Provide a `set_valid_shape` API to modify the `valid_shape` attribute of an already-allocated tile?

```mlir
      %12 = pto.make_tensor_view %arg0, shape = [%8] strides = [%c1] : !pto.tensor_view<?xf32>
      %13 = pto.make_tensor_view %arg1, shape = [%8] strides = [%c1] : !pto.tensor_view<?xf32>
      %14 = pto.make_tensor_view %arg2, shape = [%8] strides = [%c1] : !pto.tensor_view<?xf32>
      %15 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %16 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %17 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %18 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %19 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %20 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %21 = arith.cmpi slt, %11, %9 : index
      scf.if %21 {
        %22 = arith.addi %11, %10 : index
        %23 = arith.cmpi sgt, %22, %9 : index
        %24 = arith.subi %9, %11 : index
        %25 = arith.select %23, %24, %10 : index
        %26 = arith.muli %25, %c8192 : index
        %27 = arith.cmpi sgt, %26, %c0 : index
        scf.if %27 {
          scf.for %arg4 = %c0 to %25 step %c1 {
            %28 = arith.addi %arg4, %11 : index
            %29 = arith.muli %28, %c8192 : index
            %30 = pto.partition_view %12, offsets = [%29], sizes = [%c8192] : !pto.tensor_view<?xf32> -> !pto.partition_tensor_view<1x8192xf32>
            %31 = pto.partition_view %13, offsets = [%29], sizes = [%c8192] : !pto.tensor_view<?xf32> -> !pto.partition_tensor_view<1x8192xf32>
            %32 = pto.partition_view %14, offsets = [%29], sizes = [%c8192] : !pto.tensor_view<?xf32> -> !pto.partition_tensor_view<1x8192xf32>
            %33 = arith.remui %arg4, %c2 : index
            %34 = arith.cmpi eq, %33, %c0 : index
            scf.if %34 {
              pto.tload ins(%30 : !pto.partition_tensor_view<1x8192xf32>) outs(%15 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>)
              pto.tload ins(%31 : !pto.partition_tensor_view<1x8192xf32>) outs(%16 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>)
              pto.tadd ins(%15, %16 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>, !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>) outs(%17 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>)
              pto.tstore ins(%17 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>) outs(%32 : !pto.partition_tensor_view<1x8192xf32>)
            }
            %35 = arith.cmpi eq, %33, %c1 : index
            scf.if %35 {
              pto.tload ins(%30 : !pto.partition_tensor_view<1x8192xf32>) outs(%18 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>)
              pto.tload ins(%31 : !pto.partition_tensor_view<1x8192xf32>) outs(%19 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>)
              pto.tadd ins(%18, %19 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>, !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>) outs(%20 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>)
              pto.tstore ins(%20 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=8192, v_row=1, v_col=8192, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>) outs(%32 : !pto.partition_tensor_view<1x8192xf32>)
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
    return
  }
}
```

**Full frontend code to generate the IR, and kernel launch script**: https://github.com/huawei-csl/pto-dsl/pull/46

The single-buffer, dynamic-shape version works in the above PR, but has 20% performance gap vs `torch.add`. The only difference between single vs double is the additional `scf.if %34` branching and the 2x `pto.alloc_tile` calls. The dynamic `scf.for` exist in both cases.

title: Some question of dynamic shape
body:
We are using ptoas as pypto's backend, we met some issues when implementing dynamic shape:

1. Tensor 参数是否必须传入 `pto.ptr`，再在内部构造 `tensor_view`?

   ```
   func.func @kernel(%arg0: !pto.ptr<f32>, %arg1: !pto.ptr<f32>) {
       %a = pto.make_tensor_view ...
       %b = pto.make_tensor_view ...
   }
   ```

   可以在参数直接传 `tensor_view` 吗？

   ```
   func.func @kernel(%a: !pto.tensor_view<?x16xf32>, %b: !pto.tensor_view<?x16xf32>) {
       ...
   }
   ```

2. `make_tensor_view`的动态shape和stride必须是传入或计算出的 `index` 变量吗？

   ```
   func.func @kernel(%arg0: !pto.ptr<f32>, %arg1: !pto.ptr<f32>, %arg2: index) {
       %c16 = arith.constant 16 : index
       %a = pto.make_tensor_view %arg0, shape=[%arg2, %c16] ... : !pto.tensor_view<?x16xf32>
   }
   ```

   可以在 shape 中直接用 `?` 吗
   `%a = pto.make_tensor_view %arg0, shape=[?, %c16] ...`

3. 可以获取一个 `tensor_view` 的特定维度的大小吗，例如 `%a: !pto.tensor_view<?x16xf32>` 的 shape[0]

title: [Feature Request] Missing ISA instruction to retrieve tensor dimension size
body:
Currently, in the PTO-ISA, there appears to be no instruction to extract the size of a specific dimension from a tensor. For example, in the PL side, we have pl.dim(a, 0) to obtain a.shape[0], but I couldn’t find a corresponding ISA instruction.

Could you confirm if such an instruction exists? If not, would it be possible to add one to align with the PL functionality? This would greatly simplify operations that depend on dynamic tensor shapes.

title: `blayout= col_major` incorrectly emitted to `BLayout::RowMajor`, leading to wrong matmul kernel code
body:
## Problem

At today's latest commit https://github.com/zhangstevenunity/PTOAS/commit/ca7bcc852ff8ca01d418d882826951d3fd1235e2, `ptoas` EmitC generates wrong `BLayout` for cube tiles. `blayout= col_major` all become `BLayout::RowMajor`, and `slayout` all become `NoneBox` regardless of its value.  Earlier commit https://github.com/zhangstevenunity/PTOAS/commit/6a8bcdbad7a0587c1d34b035617d36f1ee9c0cfa was working correctly.

For example this part of IR:

```mlir
      %19 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=mat, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=col_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %20 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=mat, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=col_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %21 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=left, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=row_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %22 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=right, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=row_major, slayout=col_major, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %23 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=acc, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=col_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=1024, pad=0>
```

incorrectly becomes:

```cpp
  Tile<TileType::Mat, float, 128, 128, BLayout::RowMajor, 128, 128, SLayout::NoneBox, 512, PadValue::Null> v25;
  TASSIGN(v25, v15);
  Tile<TileType::Mat, float, 128, 128, BLayout::RowMajor, 128, 128, SLayout::NoneBox, 512, PadValue::Null> v26;
  TASSIGN(v26, v16);
  Tile<TileType::Left, float, 128, 128, BLayout::RowMajor, 128, 128, SLayout::NoneBox, 512, PadValue::Null> v27;
  TASSIGN(v27, v16);
  Tile<TileType::Right, float, 128, 128, BLayout::RowMajor, 128, 128, SLayout::NoneBox, 512, PadValue::Null> v28;
  TASSIGN(v28, v16);
  Tile<TileType::Acc, float, 128, 128, BLayout::RowMajor, 128, 128, SLayout::NoneBox, 1024, PadValue::Null> v29;
  TASSIGN(v29, v16);
```

The correct version should be:

```cpp
  Tile<TileType::Mat, float, 128, 128, BLayout::ColMajor, 128, 128, SLayout::RowMajor, 512, PadValue::Null> v25;
  TASSIGN(v25, v15);
  Tile<TileType::Mat, float, 128, 128, BLayout::ColMajor, 128, 128, SLayout::RowMajor, 512, PadValue::Null> v26;
  TASSIGN(v26, v16);
  Tile<TileType::Left, float, 128, 128, BLayout::RowMajor, 128, 128, SLayout::RowMajor, 512, PadValue::Null> v27;
  TASSIGN(v27, v16);
  Tile<TileType::Right, float, 128, 128, BLayout::RowMajor, 128, 128, SLayout::ColMajor, 512, PadValue::Null> v28;
  TASSIGN(v28, v16);
  Tile<TileType::Acc, float, 128, 128, BLayout::ColMajor, 128, 128, SLayout::RowMajor, 1024, PadValue::Null> v29;
  TASSIGN(v29, v16);
```

## Reproduce

Run `ptoas matmul.pto -o matmul.cpp` on this IR:

```mlir
module attributes {"pto.device-spec" = "Ascend910B1"} {
  func.func @RunTMATMULSplitK(%arg0: !pto.ptr<f32>, %arg1: !pto.ptr<f32>, %arg2: !pto.ptr<f32>, %arg3: !pto.ptr<f32>, %arg4: i1, %arg5: i32) {
    pto.section.cube {
      %c0 = arith.constant 0 : index
      %c1 = arith.constant 1 : index
      %c128 = arith.constant 128 : index
      %c128_0 = arith.constant 128 : index
      %c128_1 = arith.constant 128 : index
      %c16384 = arith.constant 16384 : index
      %c16384_2 = arith.constant 16384 : index
      %c128_3 = arith.constant 128 : index
      %c128_4 = arith.constant 128 : index
      %0 = arith.index_cast %arg5 : i32 to index
      %1 = arith.muli %0, %c128 : index
      %2 = pto.get_block_num
      %3 = arith.index_cast %2 : i64 to index
      %4 = pto.get_block_idx
      %5 = arith.index_cast %4 : i64 to index
      %6 = arith.divsi %0, %3 : index
      %7 = arith.remsi %0, %3 : index
      %8 = arith.cmpi slt, %5, %7 : index
      %9 = arith.minui %5, %7 : index
      %10 = arith.muli %5, %6 : index
      %11 = arith.addi %10, %9 : index
      %12 = arith.select %8, %c1, %c0 : index
      %13 = arith.addi %6, %12 : index
      %14 = arith.addi %11, %13 : index
      %15 = arith.minui %14, %0 : index
      %16 = pto.make_tensor_view %arg1, shape = [%0, %c128, %c128_0] strides = [%c16384, %c128_0, %c1] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?x?xf32>
      %17 = pto.make_tensor_view %arg2, shape = [%c128_0, %c128_1] strides = [%c128_1, %c1] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?xf32>
      %18 = pto.make_tensor_view %arg0, shape = [%0, %c128, %c128_1] strides = [%c16384_2, %c128_1, %c1] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?x?xf32>
      %19 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=mat, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=col_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %20 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=mat, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=col_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %21 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=left, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=row_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %22 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=right, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=row_major, slayout=col_major, fractal=512, pad=0>
      %23 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=acc, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=col_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=1024, pad=0>
      %24 = pto.partition_view %17, offsets = [%c0, %c0], sizes = [%c128_0, %c128_4] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?xf32> -> !pto.partition_tensor_view<128x128xf32>
      pto.tload ins(%24 : !pto.partition_tensor_view<128x128xf32>) outs(%20 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=mat, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=col_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>)
      pto.record_event[#pto.sync_op_type<TLOAD>, #pto.sync_op_type<TMOV_M2L>, <EVENT_ID0>]
      pto.wait_event[#pto.sync_op_type<TLOAD>, #pto.sync_op_type<TMOV_M2L>, <EVENT_ID0>]
      pto.tmov ins(%20 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=mat, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=col_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>) outs(%22 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=right, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=row_major, slayout=col_major, fractal=512, pad=0>)
      scf.for %arg6 = %11 to %15 step %c1 {
        %25 = pto.partition_view %16, offsets = [%arg6, %c0, %c0], sizes = [%c1, %c128_3, %c128_0] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?x?xf32> -> !pto.partition_tensor_view<128x128xf32>
        %26 = pto.partition_view %18, offsets = [%arg6, %c0, %c0], sizes = [%c1, %c128_3, %c128_4] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?x?xf32> -> !pto.partition_tensor_view<128x128xf32>
        pto.tload ins(%25 : !pto.partition_tensor_view<128x128xf32>) outs(%19 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=mat, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=col_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>)
        pto.record_event[#pto.sync_op_type<TLOAD>, #pto.sync_op_type<TMOV_M2L>, <EVENT_ID0>]
        pto.wait_event[#pto.sync_op_type<TLOAD>, #pto.sync_op_type<TMOV_M2L>, <EVENT_ID0>]
        pto.tmov ins(%19 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=mat, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=col_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>) outs(%21 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=left, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=row_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>)
        pto.record_event[#pto.sync_op_type<TMOV_M2L>, #pto.sync_op_type<TMATMUL>, <EVENT_ID0>]
        pto.wait_event[#pto.sync_op_type<TMOV_M2L>, #pto.sync_op_type<TMATMUL>, <EVENT_ID0>]
        pto.tmatmul ins(%21, %22 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=left, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=row_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>, !pto.tile_buf<loc=right, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=row_major, slayout=col_major, fractal=512, pad=0>) outs(%23 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=acc, dtype=f32, rows=128, cols=128, v_row=128, v_col=128, blayout=col_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=1024, pad=0>)
        pto.record_event[#pto.sync_op_type<TMATMUL>, #pto.sync_op_type<TLOAD>, <EVENT_ID0>]
        pto.wait_event[#pto.sync_op_type<TMATMUL>, #pto.sync_op_type<TLOAD>, <EVENT_ID0>]
        pto.record_event[#pto.sync_op_type<TMATMUL>, #pto.sync_op_type<TSTORE_ACC>, <EVENT_ID0>]
        pto.wait_event[#pto.sync_op_type<TMATMUL>, #pto.sync_op_type<TSTORE_ACC>, <EVENT_ID0>]

        pto.wait_event[#pto.sync_op_type<TSTORE_ACC>, #pto.sync_op_type<TMATMUL>, <EVENT_ID0>]
      }
    }
```

title: bf16 dtype in tile buffers incorrectly lowered to float in generated C++ code
body:
### Description
When processing .pto files that contain bf16 (bfloat16) typed tile buffers, ptoas incorrectly generates C++ code using float as the template type parameter instead of __bf16 (or bfloat16_t). The function signature correctly uses __bf16* for pointer parameters, but all Tile<> and GlobalTensor<> template instantiations use float for what should be bf16 data.

### Steps to Reproduce
Given the following .pto input with bf16 typed tile buffers:


```
module {
  func.func @qk_matmul(%arg0: !pto.ptr<bf16>, %arg1: !pto.ptr<bf16>, %arg2: !pto.ptr<f32>) {
    %c16 = arith.constant 16 : index
    %c128 = arith.constant 128 : index
    %c1 = arith.constant 1 : index
    %c0 = arith.constant 0 : index
    %5 = pto.make_tensor_view %arg0, shape = [%c16, %c128] strides = [%c128, %c1] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?xbf16>
    %6 = pto.make_tensor_view %arg1, shape = [%c128, %c128] strides = [%c128, %c1] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?xbf16>
    %7 = pto.make_tensor_view %arg2, shape = [%c16, %c128] strides = [%c128, %c1] : !pto.tensor_view<?x?xf32>
    %0 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=mat, dtype=bf16, rows=16, cols=128, ...>
    %1 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=mat, dtype=bf16, rows=128, cols=128, ...>
    %2 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=left, dtype=bf16, rows=16, cols=128, ...>
    %3 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=right, dtype=bf16, rows=128, cols=128, ...>
    %4 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=acc, dtype=f32, rows=16, cols=128, ...>
    // ... tload, tmov, tmatmul, tstore ...
  }
}
```
Run: ptoas qk_matmul.pto -o qk_matmul.cpp --enable-insert-sync

### Actual Behavior
The generated C++ code uses float for all bf16-typed tile buffers:


```
static __aicore__ void qk_matmul(__gm__ __bf16* v1, __gm__ __bf16* v2, __gm__ float* v3) {
  // ...
  using T = float;  // ❌ Should be __bf16 for bf16 tiles
  Tile<TileType::Mat, T, 16, 128, ...> v15;   // ❌ float instead of __bf16
  Tile<TileType::Mat, T, 128, 128, ...> v16;  // ❌ float instead of __bf16
  Tile<TileType::Left, T, 16, 128, ...> v17;  // ❌ float instead of __bf16
  Tile<TileType::Right, T, 128, 128, ...> v18; // ❌ float instead of __bf16
  Tile<TileType::Acc, float, 16, 128, ...> v19; // ✅ This one is correctly float (dtype=f32)
  // ...
  GlobalTensor<float, ...> v22 = GlobalTensor<float, ...>(v1 + ...); // ❌ float for __bf16 pointer
  GlobalTensor<float, ...> v25 = GlobalTensor<float, ...>(v2 + ...); // ❌ float for __bf16 pointer
```
Note: The function parameter types (__bf16*) are correct. The issue is specifically in the using T = ... type alias and its use in Tile<> and GlobalTensor<> template parameters.

### Expected Behavior
The generated C++ should use __bf16 (or bfloat16_t) for bf16-typed tiles and float only for f32-typed tiles:


```
static __aicore__ void qk_matmul(__gm__ __bf16* v1, __gm__ __bf16* v2, __gm__ float* v3) {
  // ...
  using T = __bf16;  // ✅ Correct type for bf16 tiles
  Tile<TileType::Mat, T, 16, 128, ...> v15;    // ✅ __bf16
  Tile<TileType::Mat, T, 128, 128, ...> v16;   // ✅ __bf16
  Tile<TileType::Left, T, 16, 128, ...> v17;   // ✅ __bf16
  Tile<TileType::Right, T, 128, 128, ...> v18; // ✅ __bf16
  Tile<TileType::Acc, float, 16, 128, ...> v19; // ✅ float (f32 accumulator)
  // ...
  GlobalTensor<__bf16, ...> v22 = ...;  // ✅ Matches __bf16* pointer
  GlobalTensor<__bf16, ...> v25 = ...;  // ✅ Matches __bf16* pointer
```
### Analysis
It appears that the C++ emitter has a single using T = ... type alias that defaults to float regardless of the actual dtype in the IR. When multiple dtypes coexist (e.g., bf16 for computation tiles and f32 for the accumulator), the emitter needs to:

Map bf16 → __bf16 (or bfloat16_t)
Map f32 → float
Either use per-tile type parameters or multiple type aliases when different dtypes are present
### Impact
This produces incorrect C++ code that will either:

Fail to compile due to type mismatches (e.g., passing __bf16* to GlobalTensor<float, ...>)
Silently produce wrong results due to incorrect memory layout assumptions (float is 4 bytes vs __bf16 is 2 bytes)

Architecture: aarch64
ptoas version: v0.2 (ptoas-bin-aarch64.tar.gz)

title: Issues with `tcvt` and `treshape` instructions in PTO bytecode due to fixed tile buffer attributes
body:
We've encountered two related issues when using the PTO bytecode with the `tcvt` and `treshape` instructions, and we'd like to discuss possible improvements.

### 1. `tcvt` instruction and memory reuse

- **Problem**: When memory reuse is enabled, the `tcvt` instruction causes an error. Disabling memory reuse makes it work correctly.

- **Root cause**: It appears that during tile buffer allocation, the data type of a tile is fixed. The type conversion required by `tcvt` cannot be performed on the same tile buffer because the buffer’s type is immutable. As a workaround, the result must be assigned to a new tile, which breaks the memory reuse optimization.

### 2. `treshape` instruction

- **Problem**: In the frontend, `treshape` is applied to a single tile (i.e., it reshapes that tile in place). However, the PTO bytecode expects different input and output tiles for this operation. This forces the compiler to generate code that uses a new output tile, which again prevents in-place reuse and may increase register/memory pressure.

### Suggestion / Feature Request

Would it be possible to enhance the PTO-isa to allow tile buffers to dynamically change their data type and shape based on the instruction being executed? This would enable operations like `tcvt` and `treshape` to work directly on a single operand (the same tile), without requiring a separate output tile. Such a change would:

- Improve memory reuse opportunities.

- Simplify the compiler backend (avoiding extra tile allocation for these operations).

- Align the bytecode behavior more closely with the frontend semantics.

title: [Feature Request] Support getval on pipe::M (CUBE core type)
body: `pto.tgetval` currently only works on Vector (V) pipe types (`MemorySpace.Vec`). When a CUBE InCore function needs to read a scalar value from a tensor (e.g., a block-table index), the tensor must be loaded into `MemorySpace.Vec`, which introduces a Vector pipe into an otherwise pure CUBE function and triggers a codegen error.

title: [Feature Request] Add layout information to tensor_view in PTO bytecode to support column‑major tile loads
body:
We have encountered a limitation in the PTO‑isa bytecode regarding the representation of tensor layouts.

### Problem

In the PTO IR, a tensor view is currently defined as:

```
%dst = pto.make_tensor_view %ptr, shape = [sh1,sh2,sh3,sh4,sh5] strides = [st1,st2,st3,st4,st5] : !pto.tensor_view<sh1xsh2xsh3xsh4xsh5xdtype>
```

However, there is no way to specify the layout of the tensor (e.g., ND vs. DN). Changing the strides does not affect the layout derivation during lowering. Consequently, in the generated CCE code, all global tensors are assumed to have ND layout. This leads to incorrect behavior when a column‑major tile is loaded from such a tensor using TLOAD – the memory access pattern is wrong.

### Suggestion

We propose extending the tensor_view type (or the make_tensor_view operation) to include an explicit layout attribute, for example layout=ND/DN. Alternatively, the layout could be inferred from the strides if the bytecode specification clearly defines how strides map to layout (currently the mapping is ambiguous).

Being able to specify the layout would ensure that the correct memory access patterns are generated during lowering, especially for operations involving column‑major tiles.

Thank you for considering this enhancement. Please let us know if there are any plans to address this or if there is a workaround we can use in the meantime.

title: [Feature] Add an install.sh script to simplify the installation process
body:
### Summary

I've been trying to install it, and I noticed that the current installation process is quite manual and error‑prone:

1. Download a pre‑compiled binary package to my local PC.

2. Upload it to the target server.

3. Extract the archive.

4. Manually set environment variables (PATH, PTOAS_ROOT, etc.).

5. Adjust file permissions (e.g., chmod +x for binaries).

This works, but it becomes tedious when deploying to multiple machines or when updating to a new version. It would be great to have an automated installation script (e.g., `install.sh`) that does all of this in one step.

### Suggested improvements

- The script could detect the operating system and architecture (Linux x86_64, aarch64, etc.) and download the appropriate pre‑built binary from the official release assets.

- It would then extract the archive to a sensible location (e.g., /usr/local or a user‑specified directory) and optionally add the binary directory to the user's PATH (by updating .bashrc/.zshrc or printing instructions).

- Permissions could be set automatically (e.g., `chmod +x` on executables).

- For convenience, the script could be made available via a one‑liner like:
```
curl -sSL https://github.com/.../install.sh | bash
```

### Motivation / use case

This would greatly lower the barrier for new users and make updates much smoother. If there are concerns about cross‑platform support, the script could initially target the most common platforms (e.g., Linux) and be extended later.

Passes / Transforms (lib/PTO/Transforms)

### Description

We have encountered an issue where the C++ code generated by PTOAS for a given PTO bytecode sequence produces incorrect results due to missing synchronization instructions. After manually inserting synchronization barriers at certain points (inspired by the CCE backend’s output), the results become correct.

### Observation

title: [Bug]  `pto.tgetval` generates an error when inputting `partition_tensor_view`
[Bug] pto.treshape lowering generates invalid C-style cast   instead of TRESHAPE macro
body:
### Component

EmitC / Codegen (lib/PTO/Transforms/PTOToEmitC.cpp)

### Description

 When PTOAS lowers `pto.treshape` operations to C++ code, it generates an
  invalid 3-line cast pattern that attempts to C-style cast a `Tile<...>`
  object to `__ubuf__ float*`. This produces a compilation error because
  `Tile<...>` is not a pointer type and cannot be cast to one.

  The correct lowering should emit a single `TRESHAPE(dst, src)` macro
  call.

### Reproduction (minimal)

1. Write a PTO bytecode program containing pto.treshape, for example
  reshaping a 16x1 col_major tile to a 1x16 row_major tile:
```mlir
  %31 = pto.treshape %3 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=16,
  cols=1, v_row=16, v_col=1, blayout=col_major, slayout=none_box,
  fractal=512, pad=0> -> !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1,
  cols=16, v_row=1, v_col=16, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box,
  fractal=512, pad=0>
```
  2. Run PTOAS to generate C++ code
  3. Attempt to compile the generated C++ code

### Expected behavior

PTOAS should generate:
```cpp
  Tile<TileType::Vec, float, 1, 16, BLayout::RowMajor, 1, 16, SLayout::NoneBox, 512, PadValue::Null> v69;
  TRESHAPE(v69, v35);
```

### Actual behavior / error logs

PTOAS generates:
```mlir
  Tile<TileType::Vec, float, 1, 16, BLayout::RowMajor, 1, 16,
  SLayout::NoneBox, 512, PadValue::Null> v69;
  __ubuf__ float* v70 = (__ubuf__ float*) v35;
  uint64_t v71 = reinterpret_cast<uint64_t>(v70);
  TASSIGN(v69, v71);
```
This fails to compile with:
```text
  error: cannot cast from type 'Tile<TileType::Vec, float, 16, 1,
  BLayout::ColMajor, 16, 1, SLayout::NoneBox, 512, PadValue::Null>' to
  pointer type '__ubuf__ float *'
      __ubuf__ float* v70 = (__ubuf__ float*) v35;
```

title: [Performance] `--enable-insert-sync` on a dynamic GEMM example generates 10% slower kernel than manual sync version
body:
### Summary

Record a practical use case where `ptoas --enable-insert-sync` still has  ~10% room for performance improvement, compared to a known manual-sync plan. 

### Background

I wrote a dynamic-shape matmul that is 2x faster than [original pto-isa `gemm_performance` example](https://gitcode.com/cann/pto-isa/tree/699931c6400b68bd19e3803eec61ad0268e2aeb0/kernels/manual/a2a3/gemm_performance) and 0.9~1.1x of [`aclnnMatmul` in CANN 8.5.0](https://www.hiascend.com/document/detail/zh/canncommercial/850/API/aolapi/context/ops-nn/aclnnMatmul.md). See [matmul_swizzle/simple_demo](https://github.com/huawei-csl/pto-dsl/tree/e7a68427ce867048ab2d43fd6847e320262bed51/examples/aot/matmul_swizzle/simple_demo) to reproduce.

The auto-sync version is [only ~100 lines of Python](https://github.com/huawei-csl/pto-dsl/blob/e7a68427ce867048ab2d43fd6847e320262bed51/examples/aot/matmul_swizzle/simple_demo/simple_matmul_builder.py#L227-L340), and reaching 90% of manual-sync is quite decent. I just wonder if the last 10% perf gap can be filled.

### Command line

```bash
ptoas --enable-insert-sync simple_matmul_auto_sync.pto -o simple_matmul_auto_sync.cpp
ptoas simple_matmul_manual_sync.pto -o simple_matmul_manual_sync.cpp
```

### Reproduction input

[pto_matmul.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25855588/pto_matmul.zip)

contains both inputs:
- `simple_matmul_auto_sync.pto`
- `simple_matmul_manual_sync.pto`

and outputs:
- `simple_matmul_auto_sync.cpp`
- `simple_matmul_manual_sync.cpp`

### Expected performance

Auto-sync should be ideally as fast as manual sync version. (or discover even faster pipelining?)

### Actual performance

Auto-sync is 5~15% slower than manual-sync, see the detailed PRs below (contains full code with kernel launch, and on-device performance measurement on 910B2:):

- Directly written in PTO-ISA C++: https://github.com/huawei-csl/pto-kernels/pull/26
- Python, manual-sync, equal performance as C++ version above https://github.com/huawei-csl/pto-dsl/pull/72
- Python, using ptoas auto-sync, 10% slower than manual sync https://github.com/huawei-csl/pto-dsl/pull/73

title: [Performance] `--enable-insert-sync` on a dynamic vector kernel (fast hadamard) generates 10% slower kernel than manual sync version
body:
### Summary

Record a practical use case where `ptoas --enable-insert-sync` still has ~10% perf gap compared to a known manual-sync plan. Similar purpose as #226, but this case is a pure vector kernel, so perhaps easier to analyze.

### Background

The chosen kernel is the NPU version of [fast-hadamard-transform](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/fast-hadamard-transform), used widely in [4-bit quantization](https://github.com/spcl/QuaRot/blob/5008669b08c1f11f9b64d52d16fddd47ca754c5a/quarot/nn/hadamard.py), in [FlashAttention-3](https://pytorch.org/blog/flashattention-3/), and also in [DeepSeek v3.2 lightning indexer](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp/blob/87e509a2e5a100d221c97df52c6e8be7835f0057/inference/model.py#L432)

See full PTO python code in [fast_hadamard](https://github.com/huawei-csl/pto-dsl/tree/e7a68427ce867048ab2d43fd6847e320262bed51/examples/aot/fast_hadamard), and performance measurement in https://github.com/huawei-csl/pto-dsl/pull/62. Auto-sync version generates 10% slower kernel than my manual plan.

### Command line

```bash
ptoas --enable-insert-sync ./hadamard_auto_sync.pto -o ./hadamard_auto_sync.cpp
ptoas ./hadamard_manual_sync.pto -o ./hadamard_manual_sync.cpp  # compare to manual sync
```

title: [Bug] TFILLPAD_EXPAND generates incorrect code when using same tile for src and dst
body:
## Description

When the input PTO bytecode has `pto.tfillpad` with the same memref for both `ins` and `outs`, ptoas generates `TFILLPAD_EXPAND(v11, v11)` using the same tile variable. This causes no padding to occur because `dstValidRow == srcValidRow`.

## Input PTO Bytecode

```mlir
%0 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=64, cols=64, 
                                     v_row=48, v_col=64, ..., pad=2>
pto.tload ins(...) outs(%0 : ...)
pto.tfillpad ins(%0 : ...) outs(%0 : ...)
...
pto.tstore ins(%0 : ...) outs(...)
```

## Current Generated Code (incorrect)

```cpp
Tile<TileType::Vec, float, 64, 64, BLayout::RowMajor, 48, 64, ..., PadValue::Max> v11;
TLOAD(v11, v14);
TFILLPAD_EXPAND(v11, v11);  // No padding happens!
...
TSTORE(v17, v11);
```

## Expected Generated Code

```cpp
// src tile: ValidRow=48, ValidCol=64 (original valid shape before padding)
Tile<TileType::Vec, float, 64, 64, BLayout::RowMajor, 48, 64, ..., PadValue::Null> v11;

// dst tile: ValidRow=64, ValidCol=64 (full shape after padding)
Tile<TileType::Vec, float, 64, 64, BLayout::RowMajor, 64, 64, ..., PadValue::Max> v12;

TLOAD(v11, v14);
TFILLPAD_EXPAND(v12, v11);  // dst=new tile (full shape), src=original tile (original shape)
...
TSTORE(v17, v12);           // Subsequent operations use the padded tile
```

## Root Cause

The `TFILLPAD_EXPAND` implementation in PTO-ISA uses `dst.GetValidRow()` as the target size for padding. When the same tile is used for both src and dst, `dstValidRow == srcValidRow`, resulting in `padRows = 0` and no padding occurs.

## Suggested Fix

For `pto.tfillpad`, ptoas should generate two separate tiles:
- **dst (new tile)**: `ValidRow/ValidCol` = full shape after padding (i.e., `Rows/Cols`)
- **src (original tile)**: `ValidRow/ValidCol` = original `v_row/v_col` before padding

All subsequent uses of the original tile should be replaced with the new dst tile.

title: pto.subset infers dynamic valid dim from dynamic offset in none_box layout, causing type mismatch
body:
## Problem
`pto.subset` type inference appears overly conservative for dynamic offsets in `none_box` layout.

When an offset is dynamic (especially dynamic column offset), inferred result type becomes dynamic in valid dims (e.g. `v_col=?`), which can conflict with explicitly annotated result types that are otherwise shape-valid.

## Repro
Environment:
- PTOAS built from this repo
- `ptoas` added to `PATH`

Command:
```bash
source env.sh
ptoas a.pto
```

Observed error:
```text
loc("a.pto":527:18): error: 'pto.subset' op inferred type(s) ... v_col=? ... are incompatible with return type(s) ... v_col=64 ...
loc("a.pto":527:18): error: 'pto.subset' op failed to infer returned types
Error: Failed to parse MLIR.
```

## Why this looks like a bug
For `none_box` view semantics, offset is the subview origin/addressing information, while valid row/col describes logical valid extent. Coupling dynamic offset directly to dynamic valid dim causes avoidable type conflicts.

In practice, moving the dynamic value from row offset to column offset path can trigger the mismatch.

## Expected behavior
`pto.subset` valid-shape inference in `none_box` should not be forced dynamic purely because offset is dynamic (or should at least be consistent with explicit result type constraints).

## Actual behavior
Dynamic offset causes inferred valid dim to become `?`, and parser/infer phase rejects IR when explicit result type carries static valid dim.

## Notes
Current `test/samples/Subset` dynamic tests may pass because they generally do not assert this specific explicit-result-type mismatch path.

```text
Error: Failed to parse MLIR.
```

---

## 最小复现用例（可直接运行）

将以下内容保存为 `subset_dynamic_mismatch.pto`：

```mlir
module {
  func.func @subset_nonebox_dynamic_mismatch(%arg0: index) {
    %c0 = arith.constant 0 : index
    %c64 = arith.constant 64 : index
    %off = arith.muli %arg0, %c64 : index

    %t0 = "pto.alloc_tile"() <{operandSegmentSizes = array<i32: 0, 0, 0>}> : () -> !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=8, cols=64, v_row=8, v_col=64, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>

    %sub = "pto.subset"(%t0, %c0, %off) <{sizes = [1, 64]}> : (!pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=8, cols=64, v_row=8, v_col=64, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>, index, index) -> !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=64, v_row=1, v_col=64, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>

    func.return
  }
}
```

运行：

```bash
ptoas subset_dynamic_mismatch.pto
```

预期触发 `v_col=?`（inferred）与 `v_col=64`（declared）冲突。

---

## 根因分析

`SubsetOp::inferReturnTypes` 当前会把 offset（尤其动态 offset）直接影响到 valid 维推导。  
这会导致 valid 维被推导成 `?`，从而和显式声明的静态 valid 维冲突。

---

## 修改建议（已验证可行）

文件：`lib/PTO/IR/PTO.cpp`  
函数：`SubsetOp::inferReturnTypes`

将 valid shape 推导改为仅基于 `sizes` 与 parent valid shape，不再使用 offset 参与计算：

- parent valid 为动态：`vdim = kDynamic`
- parent valid 为静态：`vdim = min(sizeDim, parentValidDim)`

即删除当前 offset 相关推导分支（包括对常量/非常量 offset 的特殊处理），统一为上述规则。

伪代码：

```cpp
if (parentValidDim < 0) {
  vdim = kDynamic;
} else {
  vdim = std::min(sizeDim, parentValidDim);
}
```

---

## 回归建议

新增一条测试，覆盖：
- `pto.subset` + 动态 offset + 显式静态 valid 结果类型
- 期望不再因推导 `?` 与显式类型冲突而失败

title: Need MLIR-level MC2 collective / comm-context surface and better 8-rank routing diagnostics
body:
## Summary
PTOAS can already lower local routing primitives like `TGATHER` / `TSCATTER`, but MC2 routing ports still have no MLIR-level surface for the distributed communication context itself.

## Current state
In the local 910B migration workspace:
- `moe_distribute_dispatch` and `moe_distribute_combine` now compile through `PTO-DSL -> PTOAS -> bisheng` for the real A2 contract (`epWorldSize=8`, `H=7168`).
- PTO source is explicit-sync-free and PTOAS insert-sync is active.
- The actual 8-rank routing benchmark still times out before any rank report is emitted, so failures are currently only visible at the outer harness level.

## Gaps exposed by bring-up
- No MLIR-level op or abstraction for HCCL / parallel-group / window context used by MC2 collectives.
- No direct way to represent the communication boundary in PTO IR, so MC2 ports fall back to host-managed HCCL steps outside PTOAS.
- Diagnostics for multi-rank routing failures are too indirect; once ranks stall, PTOAS provides no comm-specific breadcrumbs to distinguish context/setup issues from lowered-kernel issues.

## Requested work
- Add PTO IR / lowering surface for MC2 collective context and collective-style operations.
- Improve diagnostics around comm-lowered kernels so 8-rank routing failures can be attributed earlier and more precisely.
- Keep A2/A3 autosync behavior explicit for scalar-pipe comm instructions such as `TSCATTER`.

title: Clarify or restrict tstore_fp legality for A2/A3 vec quantized store
body:
## Summary
`pto.tstore_fp` currently looks broader at the IR/frontend layer than the backend contract it can legally lower to on A2/A3.

## Evidence
- `TStoreFPOp` in PTOAS accepts generic PTO shaped-like src/fp/dst operands.
- The verifier currently only checks:
  - src/fp/dst are PTO-shaped-like
  - src and dst have the same rank
  - src and dst have the same element type
- The A2/A3 backend contract behind `TSTORE_FP` is ACC-oriented, not a generic vec-tile quantized store.
- When trying to use it from a vec rope-cache kernel for `f16 vec -> i8 GM`, the verifier/backend path is not a legal match.

## Impact
Frontend users can reasonably infer that `pto.tstore_fp` might cover generic tile quantized store, but the current backend contract on A2/A3 does not.

## Request
Please either:
- tighten PTOAS legality/verifier/docs so `pto.tstore_fp` is clearly ACC-quantized-store only on current A2/A3, or
- extend lowering/backend support if a true vec quantized-store contract is intended.

## Affected kernels
- `rope_quant_kvcache`
- `dequant_rope_quant_kvcache`
- future rope/cache ports using int8 cache writeback

```bash
copy_outputs_as_golden
python3 "${ROOT_DIR}/golden.py"
LD_LIBRARY_PATH="${LD_LIBRARY_PATH_NPU}" "${ROOT_DIR}/${BUILD_DIR}/@EXECUTABLE@"
COMPARE_STRICT=1 python3 "${ROOT_DIR}/compare.py"
```

## Problem
For the `npu)` branch, the final comparison only needs:
1. one Python golden generation
2. one NPU execution
3. one compare step

The current flow does more work than needed:
- first `golden.py`
- first NPU run
- `copy_outputs_as_golden`
- second `golden.py`
- second NPU run
- compare

So every case pays for an extra Python golden generation and an extra NPU execution.

## Impact
This increases test latency for every generated NPU validation case.
When running many cases in batch, the redundant execution can significantly increase total validation time.

It also makes the control flow harder to understand because `copy_outputs_as_golden` is not needed if the script is going to regenerate the Python golden again before the final compare.

## Expected behavior
In `GOLDEN_MODE=npu`, the script should:
1. generate Python golden once with `golden.py`
2. run the NPU executable once
3. compare NPU output against the golden

## Suggested fix
Simplify the `npu)` branch to:
```bash
python3 "${ROOT_DIR}/golden.py"
LD_LIBRARY_PATH="${LD_LIBRARY_PATH_NPU}" "${ROOT_DIR}/${BUILD_DIR}/@EXECUTABLE@"
COMPARE_STRICT=1 python3 "${ROOT_DIR}/compare.py"
```

and remove the redundant:
- extra `golden.py`
- extra NPU run
- `copy_outputs_as_golden` call in the `npu)` branch

title: CSE incorrectly eliminates treshape on mutated tile_buf
body:
## Summary

`ptoas` CSE (Common Subexpression Elimination) incorrectly merges two `pto.treshape` operations that reference the same `tile_buf` when the buffer is mutated by an intervening `pto.trowsum` write.

## Reproduction

**Input MLIR (`.pto`)** — two `treshape %t__tile` separated by a `trowsum` that overwrites `%t__tile`:

```mlir
    // 1st row_sum: writes sum(x) into %t__tile
    pto.trowsum ins(%tile_x__tile, %tmp_tile : ...) outs(%t__tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=32, cols=1, ...blayout=col_major...>)

    // 1st reshape: reads %t__tile (contains sum(x))
    %reshape_buf = pto.treshape %t__tile : !pto.tile_buf<...rows=32, cols=1...blayout=col_major...> -> !pto.tile_buf<...rows=1, cols=32...blayout=row_major...>

    // consume %reshape_buf
    pto.tmuls ins(%reshape_buf, %cst : ..., f32) outs(%mean_T__tile : ...)

    // ... intervening ops ...

    // 2nd row_sum: OVERWRITES %t__tile with sum(centred²)
    pto.trowsum ins(%0, %1 : ...) outs(%t__tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=32, cols=1, ...blayout=col_major...>)

    // 2nd reshape: should read UPDATED %t__tile (contains sum(centred²))
    %7 = pto.treshape %t__tile : !pto.tile_buf<...rows=32, cols=1...blayout=col_major...> -> !pto.tile_buf<...rows=1, cols=32...blayout=row_major...>

    // consume %7
    pto.tmuls ins(%7, %cst : ..., f32) outs(%mean_T__tile : ...)
```

**Expected C++ output** — two separate `TRESHAPE` calls:

```cpp
TROWSUM(v32, v28, v31);       // 1st row_sum → v32
TRESHAPE(v47, v32);            // 1st reshape: v47 = reshape(v32), reads sum(x)
TMULS(v33, v47, v13);          // mean = sum(x) / N
// ...
TROWSUM(v32, v34, v35);       // 2nd row_sum → v32 (overwritten!)
TRESHAPE(v47, v32);            // 2nd reshape: v47 = reshape(v32), reads sum(centred²)  ← EXPECTED
TMULS(v33, v47, v13);          // var = sum(centred²) / N
```

**Actual C++ output** — second `TRESHAPE` is eliminated:

```cpp
TROWSUM(v32, v28, v31);       // 1st row_sum → v32
TRESHAPE(v47, v32);            // 1st reshape
TMULS(v33, v47, v13);          // mean = sum(x) / N  ✓
// ...
TROWSUM(v32, v34, v35);       // 2nd row_sum → v32 (overwritten!)
                                // ← MISSING: TRESHAPE(v47, v32)
TMULS(v33, v47, v13);          // WRONG: reads stale v47 = sum(x)/N instead of sum(centred²)/N
```

## Impact

The kernel computes `inv_std = rsqrt(mean + eps)` instead of `rsqrt(variance + eps)`, causing ~93% of output elements to be incorrect. Verified on simulator.

## Root Cause

`pto.treshape` reads from a mutable `tile_buf`. The CSE pass treats two `treshape` ops with the same source SSA name and type as identical, but does not check for intervening writes (`pto.trowsum ... outs(...)`) that mutate the source buffer between the two reads. The two `treshape` ops actually read different data and must not be merged.

## Suggested Fix

`pto.treshape` should declare a **Read** memory effect on its source operand. CSE should then verify no intervening **Write** effect exists on the same buffer before merging.

## Attachments

Full `.pto` and `.cpp` files attached below.

[layer_norm_incore_0.pto.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26131979/layer_norm_incore_0.pto.txt)

[layer_norm_incore_0.cpp](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26131976/layer_norm_incore_0.cpp)

title: TStore verifier should reject tile/partition shape mismatch and subset should not allow enlarging tile shape
body:
## Summary

`pto.tstore` currently accepts IR where the destination partition shape is larger than the source tile valid shape.

This later lowers to PTO-ISA C++ like:

```cpp
GlobalTensor<float, ..., Shape<..., 64, 64>, ...> dst = ...;
Tile<..., 64, 64, ..., 32, 32, ...> tile = ...;
TSTORE(dst, tile);
```

For PTO-ISA there is an implicit constraint: during `TSTORE`, the `GlobalTensor` shape must match the tile valid shape. The current verifier does not enforce this, so invalid IR can pass verification and only show up much later in generated code.

## Reproducer

A generated case from this repo already demonstrates the problem:

- source test case:
  `test/pto_isa_st/TMaxs/tmaxs_float_64x64_32x32_32x32.py`
- generated PTO IR:
  `build/output/TMaxs/tmaxs_float_64x64_32x32_32x32-pto-ir.pto`
- generated kernel:
  `build/output_npu_validation/TMaxs/tmaxs_float_64x64_32x32_32x32/tmaxs_float_64x64_32x32_32x32_kernel.cpp`

Relevant PTO IR:

```mlir
%4 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=32, cols=32, v_row=32, v_col=32, ...>
%5 = pto.alloc_tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=64, cols=64, v_row=32, v_col=32, ...>
%7 = pto.subset %4[%c0_5, %c0_5] sizes [64, 64] : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=32, cols=32, v_row=32, v_col=32, ...>
pto.tmaxs ins(%7, %6 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=64, cols=64, v_row=32, v_col=32, ...>, f32)
  outs(%5 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=64, cols=64, v_row=32, v_col=32, ...>)
pto.tstore ins(%5 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=64, cols=64, v_row=32, v_col=32, ...>)
  outs(%3 : !pto.partition_tensor_view<64x64xf32>)
```

This verifies today, but should be rejected earlier.

## Root cause

There seem to be two gaps:

1. `TStoreOp::verify()` checks element types / address spaces, but does not check that destination partition shape matches the source tile valid shape.
2. `SubsetOp::verify()` does not reject non-boxed subsets that enlarge the tile shape, so a `32x32` tile can become a `subset ... sizes [64, 64]`.

Because of that, invalid IR is accepted and codegen simply materializes the mismatch.

## Expected behavior

At least one of the following should be enforced:

1. `pto.tstore` verifier should reject cases where:
   - dst partition rank/shape does not match src tile valid shape
   - especially for static cases, `dst shape != src valid_shape`
2. `pto.subset` verifier should reject shape enlargement:
   - subset result sizes must not exceed source tile shape
   - ideally also remain consistent with valid-shape semantics

## Why this matters

Without this check, invalid test cases or frontend bugs can silently generate PTO IR that looks structurally valid but violates PTO-ISA constraints at `TSTORE` lowering time.

## Suggested fix

- Add a shape compatibility check in `TStoreOp::verify()`
- Add a no-enlargement check in `SubsetOp::verify()`
- Optionally add a regression test using the existing `tmaxs_float_64x64_32x32_32x32` pattern

## Local reference points

- `lib/PTO/IR/PTO.cpp`:
  - `TStoreOp::verify()`
  - `SubsetOp::verify()`
- `test/sample_utils/pto_isa_st_cases.py`:
  - `_subset_if_needed()` currently builds `pto.subset(... sizes=[dst_shape])` whenever `src_shape != dst_shape`, even when `dst_shape > src_shape`

title: [Docs] pto.tsort32 and pto.tmrgsort are incorrectly documented in PTO_IR_manual.md
body:
### Documentation location

`docs/PTO_IR_manual.md`, Section 4.11 Sorting Operations:
- `pto.tsort32` (Sort Fixed 32-Element Blocks)
- `pto.tmrgsort` (Merge Sort)

### What's wrong or missing?

Two related errors in the sort operation documentation:

#### 1. `pto.tsort32` — output format is interleaved, not two separate buffers

The manual documents `pto.tsort32` as writing two separate output buffers:

| Name | Type | Description |
|------|------|-------------|
| `dst` | `pto.tile_buf` | Sorted output |
| `idx` | `pto.tile_buf` | Index mapping output |

And the assembly format:

```mlir
pto.tsort32 ins(%src : !pto.tile_buf<...>)
           outs(%dst, %idx : !pto.tile_buf<...>, !pto.tile_buf<...>)
```

**Actual hardware behavior:** `pto.tsort32` writes a single **interleaved** buffer into `dst` of size `2N`:

```
dst = [val_0, idx_0, val_1, idx_1, ..., val_{N-1}, idx_{N-1}]
```

Where:
- `val_i` is the i-th sorted element value (`f16` or `f32`)
- `idx_i` is the permutation index stored as the same float type (`f16`/`f32`)
- Elements are in **descending** order (`val_0 ≥ val_1 ≥ ... ≥ val_{N-1}`)

So:
- `dst` has shape `[rows, 2N]` (twice the input width), not `[rows, N]`
- The `idx` output operand described in the manual is **not populated** — the hardware writes everything into `dst` in interleaved form

**Evidence:** Runtime execution of a 1×32 sort yields `dst = [2.397, 28.0, 1.465, 22.0, ...]` (values and indices alternating) rather than `dst = [2.397, 1.465, ...]` + a separate `idx = [28, 22, ...]`.

#### 2. `pto.tmrgsort` — `blockLen` is an SSA operand, not a keyword attribute

The manual shows:

```mlir
pto.tmrgsort ins(%src : !pto.tile_buf<...>) outs(%dst : !pto.tile_buf<...>) blockLen = 32
```

And describes `blockLen` as `I32Attr`.

**Actual assembly format:**

```mlir
%mrgsort_blen_64 = arith.constant 64 : i32
pto.tmrgsort ins(%src, %mrgsort_blen_64 : !pto.tile_buf<...>, i32)
            outs(%dst : !pto.tile_buf<...>)
```

`blockLen` is an **SSA value** passed as the second operand in `ins()`, not a keyword attribute.

Additionally, the physical `blockLen` passed to the hardware must be **twice** the logical block length, because the hardware counts interleaved `(value, index)` pairs — i.e., a logical block of 32 elements corresponds to a physical `blockLen = 64`.

The manual's constraint `blockLen must be a multiple of 64` is correct for the physical value, but the manual does not explain that the physical value is 2× the logical element count.

### Suggested improvement

For **`pto.tsort32`**:

1. Update the output description to show a single `dst` of width `2N` in interleaved format
2. Remove or clarify the `idx` output operand (it is not written by the hardware)
3. Add a data layout diagram showing the interleaved `[val, idx, val, idx, ...]` format
4. Clarify that element type of the index values is the same as the value type (`f16`/`f32`), not `u32`

For **`pto.tmrgsort`**:

1. Update the assembly format to show `blockLen` as an SSA operand in `ins()`
2. Clarify that `blockLen` is the physical count of interleaved pairs (= 2 × logical element count)
3. Update the argument table: change `I32Attr` to `i32 SSA value`
4. Add a note that input `src` must be in the interleaved format produced by `pto.tsort32`

title: [Feature] Improve !pto.tile_buf IR readability by eliding default fields and supporting aliases
body:
## Problem

The current custom assembly printer for `!pto.tile_buf` always prints the full parameter list:

- `loc`
- `dtype`
- `rows`
- `cols`
- `v_row`
- `v_col`
- `blayout`
- `slayout`
- `fractal`
- `pad`

This makes PTO IR very hard to read in fusion-heavy regions, because the same long type string is repeated on nearly every operand/result.

The current behavior comes from the custom parser/printer in `lib/PTO/IR/PTOTypeDefs.cpp`:

- `TileBufType::parse`: currently expects the full keyed form in a fixed order
- `TileBufType::print`: currently always emits the full keyed form

## Example

From a real IR dump in this checkout:

```mlir
pto.tmax ins(%arg9, %arg10 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=16, v_row=1, v_col=16, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>, !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=16, v_row=1, v_col=16, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>) outs(%arg11 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=16, v_row=1, v_col=16, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>)
pto.tsub ins(%arg9, %arg11 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=16, v_row=1, v_col=16, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>, !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=16, v_row=1, v_col=16, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>) outs(%arg12 : !pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=16, v_row=1, v_col=16, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>)
```

When this appears inside `pto.fusion_region`, block arguments, yields, and function-like signatures all become visually dominated by repeated type text rather than the actual dataflow.

## Why this matters

This is mainly a readability and debugging problem:

- reviewing fusion/grouping/scheduling output is slower than necessary
- IR diffs become noisy
- region signatures and `pto.yield` lines become much harder to scan
- repeated default config values hide the semantically important differences

## Suggested direction

I suggest keeping the current verbose syntax parseable for backward compatibility, but changing the default printer to a more compact form.

### 1. Elide redundant/default fields in the default printer

Possible rules:

- omit `v_row` / `v_col` when they are equal to `rows` / `cols`
- omit config fields when the config is the dialect default
  - `blayout=row_major`
  - `slayout=none_box`
  - `fractal=512`
  - `pad=0`
- compress `rows + cols + dtype` into a shaped form such as `1x16xf32`

For example:

Current:

```mlir
!pto.tile_buf<loc=vec, dtype=f32, rows=1, cols=16, v_row=1, v_col=16, blayout=row_major, slayout=none_box, fractal=512, pad=0>
```

Possible compact default:

```mlir
!pto.tile_buf<vec, 1x16xf32>
```

And when valid shape / layout differ from defaults:

```mlir
!pto.tile_buf<vec, 16x128xf32, valid=16x1, blayout=col_major>
```

### 2. Support type aliases for repeated tile_buf instances

For very repetitive IR, consider adding an `OpAsmDialectInterface` alias path so repeated identical tile types can print once and then be referenced via a short alias.

For example:

```mlir
!pto.tb0 = !pto.tile_buf<vec, 1x16xf32>
```

Then ops can use `!pto.tb0` instead of repeating the full type.

### 3. Keep a verbose/debug path available

If full information is still useful for debugging, we can keep either:

- the current syntax accepted by the parser
- an explicit verbose printing mode / debug flag

That way we improve default readability without losing inspectability.

## Expected outcome

- shorter and more readable IR dumps
- much cleaner fusion-region and block-argument printing
- lower diff noise
- no semantic change to `tile_buf`
- backward-compatible parser behavior

## Scope

This request is only about assembly syntax / textual readability. It does **not** request any change to tile semantics, layout semantics, or type invariants.

## Summary

When ptoas processes a `.pto` file containing `loc=left` tiles with `blayout=col_major`, the output C++ code incorrectly emits `BLayout::RowMajor` instead of `BLayout::ColMajor`. This causes incorrect matrix multiplication results.

## Reproduction

**Input PTO IR** — Left tiles declared with `blayout=col_major`:

```mlir
%tile_a__tile_Left = pto.alloc_tile addr = %c0i : !pto.tile_buf<loc=left, dtype=f16, rows=64, cols=64, v_row=64, v_col=64, blayout=col_major, slayout=row_major, fractal=512, pad=0>
pto.tmov ins(%tile_a__tile : !pto.tile_buf<loc=mat, ..., blayout=col_major, ...>) outs(%tile_a__tile_Left : !pto.tile_buf<loc=left, ..., blayout=col_major, ...>)
```

**ptoas command:**

```bash
ptoas gemm_incore_0.pto -o gemm_incore_0.cpp --enable-insert-sync --pto-level=level3
```

**Actual output C++** — Left tile BLayout is RowMajor (wrong):

```cpp
// line 60
Tile<TileType::Left, half, 64, 64, BLayout::RowMajor, 64, 64, SLayout::RowMajor, 512, PadValue::Null> v28;
// line 99
Tile<TileType::Left, half, 64, 64, BLayout::RowMajor, 64, 64, SLayout::RowMajor, 512, PadValue::Null> v42;
```

**Expected output C++** — Left tile BLayout should be ColMajor:

```cpp
Tile<TileType::Left, half, 64, 64, BLayout::ColMajor, 64, 64, SLayout::RowMajor, 512, PadValue::Null> v28;
Tile<TileType::Left, half, 64, 64, BLayout::ColMajor, 64, 64, SLayout::RowMajor, 512, PadValue::Null> v42;
```

## Root Cause

In the ptoas internal IR, `pto.pointer_cast` for `address_space<left>` tiles shows `blayout=#pto.blayout<row_major>`, even though the input `pto.alloc_tile` specifies `blayout=col_major`:

```mlir
// ptoas intermediate (wrong — col_major was overwritten to row_major):
%7 = pto.pointer_cast(%c0_i64) ... {config = #pto.tile_buf_config<blayout=#pto.blayout<row_major>, ...>}
    : memref<64x64xf16, strided<[64, 16], offset: ?>, #pto.address_space<left>>
```

It appears ptoas forcibly overrides `blayout` based on `address_space` rather than preserving the value from the input IR.

## Impact

Manually patching the generated C++ from `RowMajor` to `ColMajor` for Left tiles produces correct GEMM results. Without the fix, matrix multiplication outputs are entirely wrong (65531/65536 elements mismatched).

## Other Tile Types (for reference)

| TileType | blayout in PTO IR | blayout in C++ output | Correct? |
|----------|------------------|-----------------------|----------|
| Mat      | col_major        | ColMajor              | Yes      |
| Left     | col_major        | **RowMajor**          | **No**   |
| Right    | row_major        | RowMajor              | Yes      |
| Acc      | col_major        | ColMajor              | Yes      |

title: [Bug] First compilation after fresh install always times out
body:
### Diagnosis

**ptoas** — After downloading/installing a new ptoas binary, the very first compilation task always times out. Subsequent compilations work normally. This suggests a cold-start overhead issue in ptoas (e.g. lazy initialization, cache warm-up, or dynamic library loading on first run).

### Description

Every time a fresh ptoas binary is downloaded, the first compilation group encounters a 60-second timeout:

```
Failed to compile group 'qwen3_decode_layer_incore_1' [qwen3_decode_layer_incore_1_aic, qwen3_decode_layer_incore_1_aiv]: ptoas compilation timed out after 60s
```

**Steps to reproduce:**

1. Download a fresh ptoas binary from [PTOAS GitHub Releases](https://github.com/zhangstevenunity/PTOAS/releases) (e.g. `ptoas-bin-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`)
2. Extract and set `PTOAS_ROOT` to the extracted directory
3. Run any compilation that invokes ptoas, e.g. `python3 examples/models/qwen3/qwen3_32b_decode_tilelet.py` (from [pypto-lib](https://github.com/hw-native-sys/pypto-lib))
4. The first ptoas compilation group times out after 60s
5. Re-running the same script succeeds without timeout

**Workaround:** Run any trivial compilation first to "warm up" ptoas, then run the actual task.

### Environment

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| ptoas | `v0.17` |
| pypto-lib | `3acde04` |
| pypto | `50a84d7` (branch: `main`) |

### Host Platform

macOS (arm64)

### Additional Context

This issue is reproducible on every fresh ptoas install. The `ptoas --version` check also exhibits similar behavior — it times out on the first invocation (observed with a 20s timeout). This strongly suggests a one-time cold-start cost in the ptoas binary.
